title: Middle East conflict reshapes growth, resilience and partnerships across the region's largest NOCs
gist: Wood Mackenzie says the Middle East conflict has split outcomes across ADNOC, Saudi Aramco and QatarEnergy: bypass routes and a partial Hormuz reopening lifted Aramco and ADNOC combined operating cash flow by ~$35bn (25%) versus pre-war estimates, while QatarEnergy took the biggest hit just as North Field expansion was due. Capital is not the constraint; access to technology, markets and capability is, pushing NOCs toward partnerships, possible upstream opening (Aramco gas) and diversification-driven internationalisation.

insights.claim: Bypass routes, ship-to-ship shuttle transfers and a partial reopening of the Strait of Hormuz have allowed Aramco and ADNOC to raise combined operating cash flow by around $35 billion, or 25%, versus pre-war estimates.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Gulf NOCs with export flexibility are conflict winners on cash flow, supporting dividend/capex capacity.
insights.quote: increase combined operating cash flow by around $35 billion, or 25%, against pre-war estimates

insights.claim: The Aramco/ADNOC windfall is fragile: flows through the Strait of Hormuz are only partly restored, the windfall depends on elevated prices, and bypasses carry their own risks as Houthi attacks on the East-West pipeline and Red Sea shipping have shown.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Cash-flow upside is price- and route-contingent; a price normalisation or bypass disruption reverses it.
insights.quote: the recovery remains fragile and bypasses carry their own risks

insights.claim: QatarEnergy has taken the biggest hit from the conflict, just as the North Field expansion was due to lift its liquefaction capacity from 77 to 142 mmtpa.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Delays to a near-doubling of Qatari LNG capacity tighten the global LNG supply outlook versus prior expectations.
insights.quote: QatarEnergy has taken the biggest hit, just as the North Field expansion was due to lift liquefaction capacity from 77 to 142 mmtpa

insights.claim: Near term, all three NOCs are focused on restoring capacity and strengthening export resilience, while longer term the conflict will reshape business development priorities including domestic resource access, partnerships and M&A at home and abroad.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Expect a wave of NOC deal-making and partner selection once capacity is restored.
insights.locator: In the near term, all three

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's Neivan Boroujerdi says capital is not the constraint for Middle East NOCs; access to technology, markets and operational capability will shape the next phase, strengthening the role of partnerships.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: IOCs and service firms with technology and capability gain bargaining power with cash-rich NOCs.
insights.quote: Capital is not the constraint. Access to technology, markets and operational capability will shape the next phase
insights.locator: The conflict has increased the number

insights.claim: The conflict has multiplied competing demands on Gulf NOCs' capital, expertise and management attention, forcing each to balance domestic expansion, international growth and resilience simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Management bandwidth limits may slow execution and favor outsourcing to partners.
insights.quote: The conflict has increased the number of competing priorities facing Middle East NOCs
insights.locator: The conflict has increased the number

insights.claim: ADNOC, freed from OPEC quotas, is looking beyond its 5 million b/d target for 2027, with 6 million b/d mooted for the early 2030s, relying on unconventionals and additional phases at existing concessions.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Additional UAE supply outside OPEC discipline is a bearish medium-term oil supply signal.
insights.quote: Freed from OPEC quotas, it is looking beyond its 5 million b/d target for 2027, with 6 million b/d mooted for the early 2030s

insights.claim: ADNOC's global LNG platform, formed in July 2026, targets 47 mmtpa of marketable LNG by 2035, which would rank it in the top five globally on LNG capacity.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: ADNOC emerges as a major LNG portfolio player competing with majors for supply and offtake.
insights.quote: targets 47 mmtpa of marketable LNG by 2035, which would rank it in the top five globally on LNG capacity

insights.claim: Delivering oil growth, gas self-sufficiency and international expansion at once is likely to increase ADNOC's reliance on strategic partners and technical expertise.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Partnership opportunities for IOCs and service providers in UAE unconventionals and gas.

themes.theme: Aramco: gas surplus may open upstream

insights.claim: Saudi Aramco's projected sales gas supply of around 180 bcm/y in the early 2030s would outpace domestic demand of around 130 bcm/y, a surplus that could support significant LNG exports.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A ~50 bcm/y Saudi surplus would introduce a new LNG exporter into the 2030s supply picture.
insights.quote: projected sales gas supply of around 180 bcm/y in the early 2030s would outpace domestic demand of around 130 bcm/y

insights.claim: Aramco's domestic gas expansion and potential LNG exports may open part of its upstream sector to external participation for the first time.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A historic opening of Saudi upstream would be a major access opportunity for IOCs and foreign NOCs.
insights.quote: may open part of its upstream sector to external participation for the first time

insights.claim: A standalone Aramco gas entity could ring-fence gas investment from the oil business, provide a new funding vehicle for domestic gas and international LNG, and offer equity to IOCs or NOCs to facilitate LNG swaps and offtake agreements.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A carve-out structure could create an investable gas vehicle and new equity/offtake deal flow.
insights.quote: A standalone gas entity could ring-fence gas investment from the oil business

insights.claim: QatarEnergy faces the greatest strategic challenge of the three NOCs due to long-term facility damage, lost production and continued dependence on the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Qatar's lack of export bypass makes it the most structurally exposed Gulf producer.
insights.locator: QatarEnergy faces the greatest strategic challenge

insights.claim: QatarEnergy's repair costs could trigger IOC contract extensions, with ExxonMobil among the most exposed, potentially raising near-term costs for IOCs while extending their participation.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: ExxonMobil's Qatar position carries near-term cost risk but possible longer-dated participation upside.
insights.quote: Repair costs could trigger IOC contract extensions, with ExxonMobil among the most exposed.
insights.locator: QatarEnergy faces the greatest strategic challenge

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie suggests QatarEnergy should consider development-stage acquisitions alongside exploration in its international strategy, to accelerate production growth and build technical capability.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Signals QatarEnergy as a potential buyer of development-stage international assets.
insights.locator: QatarEnergy faces the greatest strategic challenge

insights.claim: The Middle East accounts for around 15% of the Majors' production today, rising to 17% by 2030, and IOC and international NOC interest will remain high because volatile environments make the region's lowest-cost barrels attractive.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Majors' growing Gulf weighting raises their sensitivity to regional geopolitical risk.
insights.quote: The region already accounts for around 15% of the Majors’ production today, rising to 17% by 2030.
insights.locator: Interest among IOCs and international NOCs

insights.claim: Elevated geopolitical risk may make some international companies more selective about Middle East exposure, so NOCs may need to widen their partnership pool to new entrants.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Opens a window for smaller or new-entrant partners to win Gulf access traditionally held by Majors.
insights.quote: NOCs may need to widen their partnership pool to new entrants
insights.locator: Interest among IOCs and international NOCs

insights.claim: Competition for non-Hormuz LNG and US gas will intensify, building on pre-war deals struck largely at or above Wood Mackenzie's base-case NPV10.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Gulf NOC buying pressure supports valuations for US gas and non-Hormuz LNG assets, risking overpayment.
insights.quote: competition for non-Hormuz LNG and US gas will intensify
insights.locator: The conflict has reinforced the strategic rationale

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie argues internationalisation by Gulf NOCs is becoming less about growth and more about resilience through diversification, with ADNOC and Aramco diversifying in gas and QatarEnergy in exploration.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Resilience-motivated buyers may pay strategic premiums rather than return-driven prices.
insights.quote: internationalisation is becoming less about growth and more about resilience through diversification
insights.locator: The conflict has reinforced the strategic rationale
